abstract: Bycatch in longline fisheries is one of the causes of population decline in albatrosses and other pelagic seabirds worldwide, and tori-lines and weighted branch lines are the mitigation measures most widely deployed to address this threat. Despite their widespread use, it remains unclear exactly how these devices reduce bycatch and whether combining them provides added protection beyond either device alone. Using experimental longline operations conducted in the western North Pacific with two albatross species commonly caught in the region, this study linked seabird attack behavior at the point of capture with the actual outcome of bycatch, revealing an overlooked mechanism. Deploying double tori-lines, rather than single, did more than reduce attacks near the vessel: it pushed birds away entirely, keeping them clear of baited hooks before capture could occur. Weighted branch lines, by contrast, reduced attacks but did not push birds away, and for one species even increased the likelihood that attacks occurred within reach of the vessel. This "stand-off effect" of a double tori-line, rather than attack suppression alone, was the strongest predictor of reduced bycatch, and its benefit did not simply add on top of the bycatch reduction by weighted branch lines. The two albatross species also responded differently to the same devices, reflecting differences in their foraging behavior. Conservation and fisheries managers designing bycatch mitigation programs should therefore evaluate candidate measures against the behavior of the seabird species actually exposed to local fishing grounds, rather than relying on standard specifications developed for different regions and species.
